lesson.title: Lactic Acid Fermentation: The Backup Plan in Burning Muscles
lesson.summary: Lactic acid fermentation regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate directly to lactate, letting glycolysis keep producing ATP in oxygen-starved muscle cells and forming the basis of foods like yogurt and cheese.
lesson.body:
Lactic acid fermentation is the simpler of the two major fermentation pathways introduced in the previous section, involving a single enzymatic step. The enzyme lactate dehydrogenase transfers electrons directly from NADH to pyruvate, reducing it to lactate and simultaneously regenerating NAD+. Unlike alcohol fermentation, no carbon is lost as CO2 in this reaction, and no intermediate like acetaldehyde is involved; pyruvate is converted straight into lactate in one move. That regenerated NAD+ then returns to glycolysis, keeping the pathway supplied and allowing the cell to continue producing its modest net 2 ATP per glucose through substrate-level phosphorylation even with no oxygen available.

The most familiar example in humans occurs in skeletal muscle during intense, short-duration exercise, such as sprinting or heavy lifting, when the demand for ATP outpaces how quickly the cardiovascular system can deliver oxygen to the working muscle fibers. Rather than stalling completely, those muscle cells shift toward lactic acid fermentation to keep glycolysis, and its ATP output, running. This is not the muscle's only or even primary source of ATP during exercise, but it is an essential supplement precisely when oxygen supply cannot keep pace with demand.

A common misconception is worth correcting, since it shows up in a lot of outdated fitness explanations: lactate buildup is not the primary cause of delayed-onset muscle soreness that appears a day or two after exercise, and lactate itself clears from the bloodstream within roughly an hour of exercise ending, too quickly to explain soreness that peaks a day or two later. Current understanding attributes that later soreness mainly to microscopic muscle fiber damage and the resulting inflammation, not to lactate. Lactate is, however, genuinely connected to the acute burning sensation felt during the exercise itself, tied to the accumulation of hydrogen ions and the resulting drop in muscle pH that accompanies intense anaerobic effort, though the exact physiological contributors to that in-the-moment fatigue remain an active area of research.

Lactic acid fermentation is not limited to muscle cells. Certain red blood cells, which lack mitochondria entirely and therefore cannot perform pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle, or oxidative phosphorylation at all, rely on lactic acid fermentation as essentially their only way of regenerating NAD+ and keeping glycolysis supplied. Certain bacteria, most notably species in the genus Lactobacillus, also rely on it as their primary energy strategy, and humans have exploited that biochemistry deliberately for thousands of years: the lactate these bacteria produce lowers the pH of milk, curdling proteins and producing the tangy taste and thickened texture of yogurt, and similar fermentation underlies many cheeses and fermented vegetables like sauerkraut.

Once oxygen supply is restored to a muscle cell, metabolism can shift back to the far more efficient aerobic pathway. The lactate that built up is not simply waste; it can be converted back to pyruvate and oxidized through pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, or transported to the liver and converted back into glucose. That recycling loop between muscle-produced lactate and liver-based glucose regeneration is known as the Cori cycle, a clear illustration that even the byproduct of an emergency, low-yield pathway like fermentation still holds recoverable chemical energy the body puts back to use.
